# ARCHITECTURE.md

A map of how this agent is put together, for humans and AI agents working in the repo. Keep it current as the codebase evolves.

## Project identification

- **Name:** eve Software Factory
- **Maintainer:** Vercel Labs (Ben Sabic)
- **License:** MIT
- **Last updated:** 2026-11-16

## Overview

This is a software factory built on the [eve](https://eve.dev) agent framework: the root agent is an orchestrator that takes work items from GitHub (an issue labeled `factory`, or an @Foreman mention), Linear (Agent Sessions), and an HTTP intake API (`POST /intake/v1/tickets`), and turns each into a draft pull request on `FACTORY_REPO`. Every item is triaged first by `triage_work_item`, a single decision-model call that classifies the item, picks labels from the repository's existing vocabulary, checks it against likely duplicates, and returns a lane: `pipeline`, `clarify`, `answer`, or `duplicate`. On the `pipeline` lane the item moves through the stations, each a declared subagent with its own instructions, sandbox, and tool surface: an optional **researcher** (web research for outside facts), the **analyst** (plan with acceptance criteria, grounded in a repo checkout), the **implementer** (executes the plan in its own checkout, runs the repo's checks, pushes a feature branch), and the **reviewer** (independent verdict on the pushed branch, different model vendor, up to 2 revision cycles). The **classifier** station is the fallback that writes clarifying questions on the `clarify` lane, or stands in when triage is unavailable. People stay in the loop where judgment lives: marking a PR ready stops the session to request approval, merging isn't in the tool surface at all, and unattended runs are denied everything except labels, progress comments on their own intake issue, closing or reopening issues, and draft PRs. Closing an issue runs ungated for every caller but one: it is reversible triage, and a reopen undoes it. The exception is the run that summarizes a pull request someone opened, which can read and comment on that pull request and nothing else. The agent runs on Vercel, the same way locally (`eve dev`) and in production (`eve deploy`).

The factory works on GitHub with the real `git` and `gh`, through each agent's `bash` tool. The orchestrator types `gh` commands there, and there is no shell behind it, on any run: one `gh` command or several joined with `&&`, with literal arguments. Each is parsed against an allowlist, checked against the caller by one policy module, and run by the app runtime itself under a per-command lease on a narrowly scoped token, reads included. The stations (analyst, implementer, reviewer) have a shell in their own sandbox, where a command gets a read-only credential at most; the implementer's `git push`, as a whole command, is run by the runtime under a lease of its own. Memory (per-user preferences and the shared factory brain) is eve's built-in file memory, recalled before every turn.

eve discovers every capability from the filesystem under `agent/`. There is no central registry or wiring file: a tool's name is its filename, a subagent's name is its directory, a memory slot's name is its filename.

## Project structure

```text
agent/
  agent.ts                  # model configuration (defineAgent): compaction threshold + a session usage limit that asks before continuing
  instructions.ts           # defineInstructions: the orchestrator prompt, resolved at build time (injects FACTORY_REPO)
  instructions/pretriage.ts # dynamic instruction: the triage result, in place before the first turn on a labeled issue or a ticket
  channels/
    github.ts               # eve GitHub channel via Vercel Connect; botName resolved from the connector's app slug; wires the four hooks from lib/github/hooks.ts and the per-turn checkout from lib/github/checkout.ts
    linear.ts               # eve Linear channel via Connect; Agent Sessions; stamps trusted (workspace membership is the gate), injects requester name
    intake.ts               # custom channel: POST /intake/v1/tickets and GET /intake/v1/tickets/:ticketId; unattended runs, optional signed callbacks
    eve.ts                  # inbound route auth; dev-only localDevUser shim (user principal, allowAgentInfo, allowToolStubs)
  connections/
    linear.ts               # Linear MCP server (mcp.linear.app); app-scoped auth via linearAuth; writes denied on unattended runs
  memory/
    preferences.ts          # slot "preferences": file memory, one document per signed-in user (userScope)
    brain.ts                # slot "brain": the factory brain, writable (trust-gated) on the orchestrator
  sandbox.ts                # root sandbox (Vercel Sandbox); the GitHub channel checks the triggering thread's ref out here, and the runtime runs the orchestrator's gh commands here
  subagents/
    classifier/             # agent.ts (tool: false) + instructions.md; text-only; writes clarifying questions, fallback when triage fails
    researcher/             # agent.ts (tool: false) + instructions.md + tools/save_artifact.ts; fresh-context web researcher
    analyst/                # agent.ts (tool: false) + instructions.md + sandbox.ts (repo clone) + memory/brain.ts (read-only) + tools/{bash,glob,grep,save_artifact,read_artifact}.ts; plans, never writes
    implementer/            # agent.ts (tool: false) + instructions.md + sandbox.ts + memory/brain.ts (read-only) + tools/{bash,glob,grep,read_artifact}.ts; the one station whose git push runs
    reviewer/               # agent.ts (different vendor, tool: false) + instructions.md + sandbox.ts + memory/brain.ts (read-only) + tools/{bash,glob,grep,read_artifact}.ts
  tools/
    agent.ts                # disableTool(): the built-in agent tool would let the root bypass its stations
    bash.ts                 # how the orchestrator runs gh: bashTool({ role: "orchestrator" }); no shell behind it, only whole gh commands, gated by bashPolicy and run by the runtime (reads under a read-only lease); it never pushes
    write_file.ts, edit_file.ts
                             # disableTool(): the orchestrator routes work and does not write code, and must not be able to write a file in the sandbox where its gh writes run
    triage_work_item.ts     # decision-model triage: classify, pick labels, check duplicates, return a lane; applies labels under the label policy
    diagnose_ci_failure.ts  # reads a PR's failing checks and logs, classifies the cause with the decision model; read-only
    run_classifier.ts, run_researcher.ts, run_analyst.ts, run_implementer.ts, run_reviewer.ts
                             # defineWorkflowTool wrappers: the model-facing entry point for each station, gated by stationPolicy. Each blocks on
                             # ctx.agent(id).send(message, { outputSchema, signal }).result() and passes the result through
                             # stationOutput(), attaching the matching schema from lib/stations/schemas.ts.
    read_artifact.ts        # Blob: read a handoff artifact by id (read-only, open to every run)
    glob.ts, grep.ts        # re-exports of eve's built-in glob and grep
  lib/
    constants.ts            # requireEnv + FACTORY_REPO/factoryRepo/FACTORY_LABEL/FACTORY_BRANCH_PREFIX + linearAuth
    models.ts               # the MODELS map: one model id per agent, plus the decision model
    trust.ts                # the single trust authority: AUTONOMOUS_PRINCIPAL, stampTrusted, stampAutonomous, stampSummary, autonomousForTicket, isAutonomous, isSummaryOnly, isTrusted, isScheduleAppAuth, intakeIssueNumber
    blob.ts                 # the Blob layer: the artifacts prefix and the private read/write document helpers
    artifacts/              # handoff artifacts: config.ts (id pattern, kinds) + tools.ts (save/read tool factories)
    stations/
      schemas.ts            # the five stations' JSON output schemas, shared by each station's run_<id>.ts wrapper
      result.ts             # stationOutput(): throws for a failed, cancelled, or empty station result
    memory/
      brain.ts              # factoryBrain({ writable }): FACTORY_REPO scope, shared namespace, trustedWrites / readOnly provider wrappers
      scope.ts              # userScope: a scope for signed-in users only, null for everyone else
    triage/
      decisions.ts          # the decision-model question sets and thresholds: triageWorkItem, laneFor, diagnoseCiFailure
      github.ts             # the gh reads and writes triage needs: fetchIssue, fetchLabels, findDuplicateCandidates, applyLabels, fetchChecks, fetchFailedLogs
      ci.ts                 # diagnosePullRequestChecks: a pull request's check status and, when a failed log can be read, its cause
      run.ts                # runTriage: read the item, ask the decision model, apply its labels; shared by the tool and pre-triage
      pretriage.ts          # triage before the orchestrator's first turn: which runs get it, and the instruction it writes
    intake/
      ticket.ts             # the ticket schema, ticket id and caller-bound address derivation, callback allowlist, HMAC signature helpers, publicError, readLimitedText
      callbacks.ts          # the signed status callbacks: turnSettledCallback, interactionOpenedCallback, sessionEndedCallback, postCallback
    github/
      credentials.ts        # GITHUB_CONNECTOR + the shared Connect credentials handle for the channel and the session clone
      cli.ts                # parseGh: the gh argv allowlist (COMMANDS) and the effect each invocation reduces to; GH_WRITE_COMMANDS; the command line and PATH the runtime runs gh with
      shell.ts              # analyzeCommand: sorts a bash command into plain, shell, gh, or push; the literal-word lexer; inlineBodyFiles
      shims.ts              # ghShim and gitShim: the gh and git wrapper scripts seeded into every sandbox, and the variables the bash tool exports for them
      git-cli.ts            # parseGitPush and pushCommandLine: git push, which the runtime always runs itself, against the literal repository URL; parseGitFetch, for a deployment that cannot issue a read-only token; rewriteGuard, which stops the runtime's git commands when a git config file rewrites URLs
      approval.ts           # the one policy module: bashPolicy, shellDecision, shellAvailable (the stations have a shell, the orchestrator does not), stationPolicy, ghEffectDecision, the per-effect decisions, factoryBrainPolicy
      lease.ts              # credential leases: scoped token minting (TOKEN_SCOPES), firewall placeholder swap, withShellLease, runGh, runGitPush, runGitFetch, runLeasedGitCommand
      tools.ts              # bashTool: eve's bash wrapped with the sorter, the leases, and the runtime's own gh and push runners; mounted by the orchestrator and the stations
      tooling.ts            # installFactoryTooling (gh, pnpm, and the wrappers in sandbox prepare) and FACTORY_TOOLING_VERSION, a digest of the install script
      checkout.ts           # checkoutForTurn: the orchestrator's per-turn checkout under a read-only lease, in place of the channel's default
      hooks.ts              # the GitHub channel's dispatch hooks and injected tasks: onComment, onIssue, onCheckSuite, onPullRequest
      git-remote.ts         # validateRef, validateBranch, REMOTE_URL, REPO_DIR, mintInstallationToken (the lease ladder's last rung, used only when FACTORY_TOKEN_FALLBACK=installation)
      repo-sandbox.ts       # FACTORY_SANDBOX_CREATE_OPTIONS, createFactoryEnvironment, factoryOpenOptions (the egress policy), factoryInit (install scripts off, clone, setup command, per session)
      egress.ts             # basePolicy and withBasePolicy: the allowlist every sandbox opens with and every lease is laid over; FACTORY_SANDBOX_EGRESS, FACTORY_SANDBOX_ALLOWED_DOMAINS
      install-scripts.ts    # the command that turns package install scripts off in a station session; FACTORY_ALLOW_INSTALL_SCRIPTS
      push-signed.ts        # PUSH_SIGNED_SCRIPT: the push as commits GitHub signs, through the Git Data API; FACTORY_SIGNED_COMMITS
      bot-name.ts           # resolves the @mention name from FACTORY_BOT_NAME or the connector's app slug
      bootstrap-diagnostics.ts # turns clone and token failures into messages that name FACTORY_REPO and the fix
  skills/                   # load-on-demand procedures, routed by description frontmatter
    writing-quality/        # AI-tells, plain English, prose specs
    triaging-issues/        # grounding a GitHub work item: dedupe, repo-native labels, ask-or-proceed, repro requests
    github-linear-bridging/ # bridged Linear issues: dedupe check, backlinks, team choice, two-way links
evals/                      # eve eval runner suite: smoke, routing/, safety/, pipeline/ (opt-in real run), helpers.ts, evals.config.ts
tests/                      # vitest suite, deterministic and offline: github/, intake/, lib/, memory/, stations/, surface/, triage/, types/, helpers.ts
scripts/                    # discovery.ts (runs eve info --json and parses the report) + check-discovery.ts (pnpm run discovery)
vitest.config.ts            # test configuration: placeholder env for modules that validate it at load
```

## Core components

| Component | Lives in | eve primitive | Responsibility |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Orchestrator | `agent/agent.ts` + `instructions.ts` | Agent | Triages each work item, routes it through the stations in order, verifies handoffs, runs the review loop (max 2 cycles), opens the draft PR, reports back; never writes code itself |
| GitHub surface | `agent/channels/github.ts` + `agent/lib/github/hooks.ts` | Channel | Intake and delivery: association-gated @Foreman mentions (stamped trusted), `factory`-label intake (rewritten to the autonomous principal, unattended framing injected), red-CI fix runs on `factory/*` PRs, PR summary comments on opened PRs (stamped summary-only); replies render in-thread |
| Linear surface | `agent/channels/linear.ts` | Channel | Linear Agent Sessions: users delegate issues to the factory; every session is stamped trusted (workspace membership); elicitations render natively |
| Intake API | `agent/channels/intake.ts` + `agent/lib/intake/ticket.ts` + `agent/lib/intake/callbacks.ts` | Channel (custom) | Tickets in over HTTP: authenticates the caller, validates a strict schema, starts an unattended session under the autonomous principal, reports status and the final message, optionally POSTs signed callbacks |
| Route auth | `agent/channels/eve.ts` | Channel | Inbound auth for the eve route; the `localDevUser` shim upgrades the dev principal to a user so user-scoped memory works in the dev TUI, and keeps `/eve/v1/info` and tool stubs available to local `eve eval` |
| `bash` tool | `agent/lib/github/tools.ts`, mounted at `agent/tools/bash.ts` and each repo station's `tools/bash.ts` | Tool | The GitHub surface: eve's `bash`, wrapped, so agents run the real `git` and `gh` in the mounting agent's sandbox. On a station a shell command gets a read-only lease at most, and a `git push` (implementer only) is run by the runtime instead. The orchestrator has no shell: every command must be a whole `gh` list, which the runtime runs, reads and writes alike |
| Command sorter | `agent/lib/github/shell.ts` | Library | Sorts each `bash` command into `plain`, `shell`, `gh`, or `push`, which decides the credential it can get; a command it does not fully understand is `shell`, which cannot write |
| Argv allowlists | `agent/lib/github/cli.ts`, `agent/lib/github/git-cli.ts` | Library | Parse a `gh` command against a fixed table of commands and flags, pin it to `FACTORY_REPO`, and reduce it to one effect; accept one form of `git push`; anything unlisted is refused with a reason |
| Authorization policy | `agent/lib/github/approval.ts` | Library | The one place an effect and a caller class become run, wait for approval, or denied, and the place that says which agents have a shell (`shellAvailable`: the stations do, the orchestrator does not); also holds the station tools' policy and the brain's write policy |
| Credential leases | `agent/lib/github/lease.ts` | Library | Mints a repository- and permission-scoped installation token per command, hands the process a placeholder, and has the sandbox firewall swap it in; resets the policy afterwards |
| Decision-model triage | `agent/tools/triage_work_item.ts`, `agent/tools/diagnose_ci_failure.ts` + `agent/lib/triage/` | Tools | Fast, closed-question judgments through eve's `decide`: classification, label selection, duplicate check, lane; and the cause of a red CI run |
| Trust authority | `agent/lib/trust.ts` | Library | The only place caller trust is defined: trusted (stamped at dispatch), autonomous (label intake, CI fixes, intake tickets), summary-only (the autonomous principal narrowed for a pull request anyone opened), schedule app auth; new capabilities gate on these predicates rather than inventing their own checks |
| classifier | `agent/subagents/classifier/` + `agent/tools/run_classifier.ts` | Subagent | Language-model classification that also writes the clarifying questions; called on the `clarify` lane or when triage fails |
| researcher | `agent/subagents/researcher/` + `agent/tools/run_researcher.ts` | Subagent | Fresh-context web research for facts the repo and tracker don't hold, called through its workflow-tool wrapper; returns cited findings + gaps |
| analyst | `agent/subagents/analyst/` + `agent/tools/run_analyst.ts` | Subagent | Planning against its own repo checkout, called through its workflow-tool wrapper; returns problem statement, approach, plan, risks, acceptance criteria, test strategy |
| implementer | `agent/subagents/implementer/` + `agent/tools/run_implementer.ts` | Subagent | Implementation in its own checkout, called through its workflow-tool wrapper: branch, code, run the repo's checks, commit, `git push`; returns branch + change summary + verification |
| reviewer | `agent/subagents/reviewer/` + `agent/tools/run_reviewer.ts` | Subagent | Independent review on a different vendor, called through its workflow-tool wrapper: `git fetch` the branch, read the real diff, judge each acceptance criterion; returns approve/request_changes/reject |
| Linear access | `agent/connections/linear.ts` | Connection (MCP) | Create issues, comment, cross-reference; app-scoped auth via `linearAuth`; denied on unattended runs |
| User preferences | `agent/memory/preferences.ts` + `agent/lib/memory/scope.ts` | Memory slot | Per-user standing preferences in eve file memory, scoped to the resolved `user` principal (never model input); off for every other caller. Tools: `preferences__save_memory`, `preferences__remove_memory` |
| Factory brain | `agent/memory/brain.ts`, `agent/subagents/{analyst,implementer,reviewer}/memory/brain.ts` + `agent/lib/memory/brain.ts` | Memory slot | Shared, durable notes about the target repository, scoped to `FACTORY_REPO`; recalled by the orchestrator and the three repo stations, written only on the orchestrator through `brain__save_memory` / `brain__remove_memory` under `factoryBrainPolicy` |
| Handoff artifacts | `agent/lib/artifacts/` + per-station `tools/{save,read}_artifact.ts` + root `agent/tools/read_artifact.ts` | Tools | Long Markdown documents stations pass by id in Blob: researcher and analyst save, analyst/implementer/reviewer read, the orchestrator relays only the id; ids validated by an anchored pattern so they can't escape the reserved prefix |
| Sandbox tooling | `agent/lib/github/tooling.ts` + `agent/lib/github/shims.ts` + `agent/lib/github/repo-sandbox.ts` | Sandbox | Installs `gh` and pnpm and seeds the `gh` and `git` wrappers into `/usr/local/bin` once per template snapshot (`prepare`); clones `FACTORY_REPO` and runs `FACTORY_SETUP_COMMAND` once per station session (`factoryInit`) |
| Skills | `agent/skills/` | Skill | Load-on-demand procedures: `writing-quality`, `triaging-issues`, `github-linear-bridging` |
| Tests | `tests/` | Vitest | Deterministic, offline checks of the allowlists, the command sorter, the wrappers, the authorization matrix, leases, hooks, trust stamps, memory, triage, the intake API, station schemas, and the assembled surface |
| Evals | `evals/` | Evals | eve eval runner: routing and safety assertions against a real model (read-only cases are deny-by-default: a `bash` command that is a `gh` list with a step that doesn't parse as an allowlisted read, or a `git push`, fails them), an opt-in full-pipeline run |

Channels and the connection are I/O boundaries. Tools run in the app runtime (full `process.env`); the `bash` tool runs its commands inside the mounting agent's sandbox. Skills only add instructions to context. Every station sets `tool: false` and is called through its `run_<id>` workflow tool, which blocks on `ctx.agent(id).send(message, { outputSchema, signal }).result()`, so the orchestrator still gets structured output back from a single call; a failed or cancelled station surfaces as a tool error through `stationOutput()`. Nothing in a station's own tool surface may need approval, since nobody is watching that station's card (see Security considerations).

## Data flow

1. **Unattended intake (`factory` label):** a maintainer labels an issue `factory`. The `issues` webhook hits `onIssue`, which dispatches only on the `labeled` action and only after verifying the labeler holds at least triage permission on the repository (GitHub fires `labeled` even for labels attached at creation, which issue templates let unauthenticated reporters do). The session's auth is rewritten to the constructed autonomous principal, and an injected task frames the run: never ask, post questions and stop if clarification is needed, deliver a draft PR. The pipeline runs; the orchestrator opens the draft PR (`gh pr create --draft` needs no approval) and announces it in the closing reply the channel delivers to the issue.
2. **Unattended intake (HTTP ticket):** a caller POSTs a ticket to `/intake/v1/tickets`. The channel authenticates the caller (a Vercel OIDC token for the project, the `FACTORY_INTAKE_TOKEN` bearer, or `localDev()` in `eve dev`), validates the body against a strict schema, derives a ticket id, and starts a session at the address `ticket:<digest of caller>:<ticketId>` under the autonomous principal built by `autonomousForTicket`. It answers `202` with `ticketId`, `sessionId`, and `deliveryId`; resubmitting the same `externalId` from the same caller answers `200` with `duplicate: true` and the original session. There is no issue thread, so the run posts no comments: its final message (the draft PR link, or the clarifying questions) is the result, read with `GET /intake/v1/tickets/:ticketId`, which reports `queued`, `running`, `awaiting-input`, `completed`, `failed`, or `cancelled`. The address carries the caller, so a ticket is bound to the caller that submitted it: the same GET from another caller is a `404`. A ticket is one run, so an answer to clarifying questions arrives as a new ticket with a new `externalId`. With an allowlisted `callbackUrl` and a configured secret, the channel also POSTs signed updates when a turn settles, an interaction opens, or the session fails; a `callbackUrl` with no secret configured is refused with `400` `callback_not_configured`.
3. **Red CI on a factory PR:** a `check_suite` webhook with a failure conclusion, anchored to a pull request whose head branch starts with `factory/`, hits `onCheckSuite`. The session runs unattended on that PR's thread. The injected task self-limits: count earlier fix-attempt comments on the PR (each fresh session's only shared memory is the thread), stop and hand off to a person after 2. Otherwise it calls `diagnose_ci_failure`, which reads the checks and failed-step logs with `gh` (`diagnosePullRequestChecks`) and returns a `status`: `passing`, `pending`, `cancelled`, or `no-checks` when nothing is failing, `failing` when a failed log was read and the decision model judged its cause, and `failing-no-log` when something failed and no log could be read. `fix_with_code` is true, false, or null. Only when it is true does the run post an attempt comment and send an implementer/reviewer revision that pushes to the same branch; when it is false on a `failing` status (a flaky, infrastructure, or configuration failure) the run posts one explanatory comment and makes no fix attempt. Null comes only with `failing-no-log` and means the cause is unknown, never that the code is fine: the run names the failing checks, says their logs weren't readable, and asks a person to look. When nothing is failing the run stops without posting. Suites on branches people pushed never dispatch.
4. **Attended intake (@Foreman mention):** `onComment` keeps the built-in mention and ignore rules, dispatches only for OWNER/MEMBER/COLLABORATOR commenters, and stamps `attributes.trusted`. The pipeline runs with the requester on the other end: clarifying questions go to them, reversible writes run without cards, shipping actions stop and wait for approval.
5. **Linear sessions:** a user delegates an issue in Linear; `onAgentSession` stamps trusted and injects the requester's name. The factory works the item, posts progress as Agent Activities, and reports the PR link back on the session. Cross-tracker conventions come from the `github-linear-bridging` skill.
6. **The pipeline itself:** the orchestrator reads the real work item, then calls `triage_work_item` (with `issue_number` for a GitHub issue, or the title and body verbatim otherwise). The tool reads the issue, the repository's labels, and duplicate candidates with `gh`, asks one decision-model call for the classification, a yes/no per existing label, and a yes/no per candidate, applies the selected labels, and returns the lane, along with `labels_not_considered`: how many repository labels the model was not asked about (beyond the limit of 40, or left out because a comma in the name means `gh` could not apply it). `clarify` goes to the classifier for the questions to ask, `answer` is answered without building, `duplicate` is checked by the orchestrator before it acts, and `pipeline` delegates in order: optional researcher (when `needs_research` is true) → analyst (reads its checkout) → implementer (branches, implements, verifies, pushes with `git push`) → reviewer (fetches the branch, judges the real diff). `request_changes` loops back to the implementer at most twice. Every delegation message is self-contained; stations never see the orchestrator's history, though the analyst, implementer, and reviewer recall the factory brain themselves. Long documents skip the inline path: the researcher and analyst can save a handoff artifact and return its id in `artifact_id`, the orchestrator relays the id, and downstream stations read the document themselves with `read_artifact`.
7. **A GitHub command, end to end:** the model calls `bash` with an ordinary command line, and `analyzeCommand` (`agent/lib/github/shell.ts`) sorts it into one of four kinds, once in the tool's approval function and again when it executes. How a kind runs also depends on the agent. `shellAvailable(role)` (`agent/lib/github/approval.ts`) is true for a station and false for the orchestrator, whoever the caller is. On the orchestrator only the `gh` kind below is accepted, one `gh` command or several joined with `&&`, and the runtime always parses and runs it itself, reads included. Any other command (a pipe, `ls`, `git status`, a script) is denied with the `GH_ONLY` message, and the tool's `execute` refuses it again before any shell call or token mint. The `plain` and `shell` kinds, and the shell path for a `gh` list of reads, are the stations'.
   - `plain` names neither `gh` nor a networked `git` command (`fetch`, `pull`, `push`, `clone`, `ls-remote`). On a station it runs in eve's `bash` as is, with no credential. The check for a networked git command is loose on purpose: it looks for one of those words between `git` and the end of that command, so `git stash push` counts, and gets a read-only credential it does not use.
   - `shell` names one of them, in any shape: a pipe, a variable, a script. On a station the policy lets it run, in the shell, under a read-only lease. `withShellLease` mints a `repo-read` token, strictly (`FACTORY_TOKEN_FALLBACK` never widens it; token scopes under Security say what happens when no read-only token can be issued), sets a firewall policy that swaps a random placeholder for it on `api.github.com`, `uploads.github.com`, `github.com`, and `codeload.github.com`, and resets the policy in a `finally`. The tool prepends one `export` line to the command (`FACTORY_GITHUB_LEASE`, `FACTORY_REPO`, `FACTORY_GITHUB_ROLE`). The names `gh` and `git` resolve to the wrappers in `/usr/local/bin`, which hand the placeholder to the real programs.
   - `gh` means the whole command is a list of `gh` commands with literal arguments, joined by `&&`, `;`, or new lines. A list in which `gh` is asked about itself (a bare `gh`, `gh help`, `gh version`, `gh -h`, or any `gh` command with `--help` or `--version`) is `shell` instead: on a station it needs no approval, and the wrapper passes it to the real `gh`. The approval function denies a list of more than 12 commands (`MAX_GH_STEPS`) and passes each step through `inlineBodyFiles` and `parseGh`. A step the allowlist refuses denies the command with the reason. On the orchestrator each step's effect goes through `ghEffectDecision` for the caller's class and the strictest outcome decides for the list; on a station anything but a read is denied. A step that would wait for a person's approval may not use `--body-file`: the file is read when the command runs, after the approval, so the approver could not see the text, and the command is denied with a reason that says to use `--body`.
   - A `gh` list runs one of two ways. On a station, a list of reads runs in the shell, exactly like a `shell` command. On the orchestrator every list, reads and writes alike, is not run by a shell at all: `runGhSteps` runs the parsed words one step at a time, honouring `&&` and `;` as a shell does (after a failed step, a step joined with `&&` is skipped and a step after a later `;` still runs). It reads any `--body-file` text from the sandbox itself with a bounded read (`/usr/bin/head -c`, one byte past the body limit) and refuses the step when the file is missing or too long. The file's text is contributor-controlled and is read after the policy judged the command, so the step is parsed again with the text in and runs only when it is still the command that was approved, word for word apart from the body. For `issue close` and `issue reopen` it first asks GitHub whether the number is a pull request and refuses if it is, or if it cannot tell. A step refused at this stage fails the whole command when no step has run yet; once an earlier step has run, the result reports that step as failed (exit code 1, the reason on stderr) and keeps the earlier output, so the agent does not repeat a comment that was already posted. For each step `runGh` mints a token (`repo-read` for a read, `repo-triage` for a write), writes every body to a temp file of its own and passes `--body-file`, sets a firewall policy that swaps the placeholder on `api.github.com` and `uploads.github.com`, runs `/usr/bin/gh` with `GH_TOKEN` set to the placeholder, `GH_REPO` set to `FACTORY_REPO`, and `PATH` set to `/usr/bin:/bin` (which skips the wrappers), and resets the policy in a `finally`.
   - `push` means the whole command is one `git push` (`cd repo && git push ...` and `git -C repo push ...` are also read as one). It is denied unless the caller is the implementer, the directory is the station's checkout, and `parseGitPush` accepts the words. It is not run by a shell either: when no branch is named the tool reads the checked-out branch and validates it, then `runGitPush` runs `/usr/bin/git push` against the literal repository URL under a `repo-push` lease, once `rewriteGuard` has found no `url.*` rewrite in git's config files, with the placeholder carried in git's own config through the environment and swapped on `github.com` and `codeload.github.com`.

   Output is redacted for the exact leased token. Output of a command the runtime runs itself is also truncated before the model sees it (`run view` keeps the tail, every other command the head).
8. **PR opened (by someone else):** `onPullRequest` dispatches on the `opened` action (bot senders skipped, which covers `foreman[bot]`'s own PRs) with a summary task injected and the session stamped summary-only (`stampSummary`); the agent posts one orienting comment with a changed-files table, and can do nothing else.
9. **Learning:** when a run surfaces a durable fact about the repository, the orchestrator saves it to the brain with `brain__save_memory`. An unattended run has no brain tools, so it puts the fact in its final reply as a suggested note for a maintainer to record.

## Data stores

- **GitHub** (external): the repository and issue tracker the factory works on. Access goes through the `gh` and `git` binaries in sandboxes, authenticated at the sandbox firewall with installation tokens minted through Vercel Connect (see Security).
- **Linear** (external): where delegated work arrives and cross-references land. Access via Linear's MCP server with app-scoped Connect auth (scopes `read`, `write`, `issues:create`, `comments:create`).
- **eve file memory**: the `preferences` documents (one per signed-in user) and the `brain` document (one per `FACTORY_REPO`). Deployed, eve stores them in a private Vercel Blob store connected under the `EVE_MEMORY_BLOB` prefix (`eve integration setup file-memory` provisions it and sets `EVE_MEMORY_BLOB_STORE_ID`); when that is absent eve falls back to the application's own Blob configuration (`BLOB_STORE_ID` or `BLOB_READ_WRITE_TOKEN`). In `eve dev` the documents live in process-local memory and are gone when the process exits. eve recalls each document before every turn; one entry is at most 2,048 bytes and a stored document at most 65,536 bytes, and the brain's recalled message is capped at 8,000 characters.
- **Vercel Blob** (the application's store, private): handoff artifacts under the reserved `artifacts/<validated-id>.md` prefix, reachable only through the artifact tools. The store is provisioned private and every read and write uses private access (`agent/lib/blob.ts`), so a document is never readable by its URL. Authenticated by the project's OIDC token.
- **Session and channel state** (eve): the intake channel keeps `ticketId` and `callbackUrl` as per-session channel state, and a ticket's status is derived from its session's recorded events. There is no ticket table.
- **Vercel Sandbox**: the root sandbox holds the GitHub channel's thread checkout and is where the runtime runs the orchestrator's `gh` commands; each repo-facing station's sandbox holds its own clone of `FACTORY_REPO`, cloned fresh per session by `factoryInit`. Template snapshots carry the installed tooling (`gh`, pnpm, the `gh` and `git` wrappers), not the repository. Not durable application stores.

There is no application database. Anything that must outlive a session (for example, cross-run sweep state for a future schedule) belongs in an external store.

## External integrations

| Integration | Purpose | Method |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GitHub | Label intake, mentions, CI and PR events in; comments, labels, branches, and draft PRs out | eve GitHub channel via Vercel Connect (`GITHUB_CONNECTOR`); the `gh` and `git` binaries in sandboxes, with per-command installation tokens from `@vercel/connect` `getToken` swapped in at the sandbox firewall |
| Linear (channel + MCP) | Agent Sessions in; issue creation, comments, cross-references out | eve Linear channel via Connect; MCP connection to `mcp.linear.app` with app-scoped auth shared through `linearAuth` (`LINEAR_CONNECTOR`) |
| Intake API callers | Tickets in over HTTP, status out, optional callbacks out | Custom channel routes `POST /intake/v1/tickets` and `GET /intake/v1/tickets/:ticketId`; bearer secret or Vercel OIDC; callbacks signed with HMAC-SHA256 |
| Vercel Blob | eve file memory (preferences, factory brain) and station handoff artifacts | eve's file-memory backend for memory; `@vercel/blob` for artifacts; OIDC-authenticated |
| Vercel AI Gateway | Model access for the root, every station, and the decision model | Gateway model ids, all in `agent/lib/models.ts` (the reviewer deliberately runs a different vendor than the implementer; `decision` is `typesafe-ai/jev`) |
| Vercel Sandbox | Isolated runtimes: root checkout + three station clones | `agent/sandbox.ts` and `agent/subagents/*/sandbox.ts` (`VercelSandbox.environment()`, shared options and builders in `agent/lib/github/repo-sandbox.ts`) |

## Deployment & infrastructure

- **Platform:** Vercel, Node 24. Deploy with `eve deploy` (wraps `vercel deploy --prod`; the raw command cannot auto-detect the eve framework).
- **Connectors:** provisioned via `vercel connect create` + `attach`; the GitHub trigger points at `/eve/v1/github` (subscribe to `issues`, `issue_comment`, `pull_request_review_comment`, `pull_request`, and `check_suite`) and the Linear trigger at `/eve/v1/linear` (AgentSessionEvent).
- **GitHub App permissions:** the installation needs write access to contents, issues, and pull requests on `FACTORY_REPO`. CI diagnosis (`gh pr checks`, `gh run view --log-failed`) also needs Actions read and Checks read. The factory requests those two together with Commit statuses read as one optional group, and drops the whole group for a token when the installation refuses any of them, so grant all three. Workflows write is requested only when `FACTORY_ALLOW_WORKFLOW_CHANGES=1` is set; without it the push token cannot change `.github/workflows`, and GitHub rejects a push that tries. The factory asks for less than the app holds on each command (see token scopes under Security), so granting a permission does not hand it to every command.
- **Memory storage:** run `eve integration setup file-memory` in the linked project, then redeploy. It creates or reuses a private Blob store, connects it with the `EVE_MEMORY_BLOB` prefix, and sets `EVE_MEMORY_BLOB_STORE_ID`; there is nothing to fill in by hand.
- **Intake routes:** `POST /intake/v1/tickets` and `GET /intake/v1/tickets/:ticketId` are served by the same deployment. Set `FACTORY_INTAKE_TOKEN` (at least 32 characters) to let callers outside Vercel submit; leave it unset and only callers holding a Vercel OIDC token for the project can.
- **Environment:** connector UIDs `GITHUB_CONNECTOR` and `LINEAR_CONNECTOR`; `FACTORY_REPO` (required at module load; a missing value fails discovery). Optional: `FACTORY_SETUP_COMMAND` (runs inside the clone once per station session), `FACTORY_LABEL`, `FACTORY_BRANCH_PREFIX` (default `factory/`; the only branches the implementer can push to), `FACTORY_BOT_NAME`, `FACTORY_INTAKE_TOKEN`, `FACTORY_INTAKE_CALLBACK_HOSTS` (comma-separated `host` or `host:port` entries callbacks may go to), `FACTORY_INTAKE_CALLBACK_SECRET` (signs callbacks; none are sent without it), `FACTORY_TOKEN_FALLBACK` (unset or `none` fails closed when a narrowed token is refused; `repository` or `installation` allow wider tokens for the commands the runtime runs itself, never for a shell command, see Security), `FACTORY_ALLOW_WORKFLOW_CHANGES` (`1` adds Workflows write to the push token), `FACTORY_SANDBOX_EGRESS` (unset holds every sandbox to an allowlist of GitHub and the public package registries; `open` allows every host), `FACTORY_SANDBOX_ALLOWED_DOMAINS` (comma-separated hostnames added to that allowlist, exact match, no wildcards), `FACTORY_ALLOW_INSTALL_SCRIPTS` (`1` lets package managers run install scripts in station sandboxes), and `FACTORY_SIGNED_COMMITS` (`1` delivers branches as commits GitHub signs, through the Git Data API). The model and Blob authenticate via the project's OIDC token.
- **Local development:** `pnpm dev` runs the same runtime in a TUI; `vercel env pull` supplies a short-lived OIDC token (needed for Connect and the sandboxes). The webhook surfaces run against a deployment; point the TUI at one with `eve remote connect --url <url>`. The dev principal is untrusted by design, so approval cards surface in the TUI. Memory is process-local in `eve dev`.

## Security considerations

- **Trust is decided at dispatch, not in the prompt.** The channel hooks decide who the caller is on the signed webhook (or the authenticated intake request) and stamp it into session auth (`attributes.trusted`, or the constructed autonomous principal). `agent/lib/trust.ts` is the single authority reading those stamps; a new capability never invents its own caller check.
- **Three caller classes, one policy module.** `agent/lib/github/approval.ts` returns `not-applicable` (run), `user-approval` (stop and wait for a person), or `denied`. Unattended runs (label intake, CI fixes, intake tickets) are denied rather than left waiting: nobody is watching to answer, and a server-side denial costs one step instead of a stranded session. Trusted callers (a stamped mention, a Linear session, a schedule turn) run routine reversible writes without a prompt. Everyone else (the dev TUI, an unstamped session) waits for a person on writes. A summary-only run is the unattended class narrowed further, for a pull request opened by anyone: it may read, and comment on that one pull request, and is denied everything else, including labels, closing or reopening issues, draft PRs, and starting any station (`stationPolicy` is the `approval` of every `run_<id>` tool).
- **A shell command never holds a credential that can write.** The orchestrator and the three repo stations all mount the wrapped `bash`. The orchestrator has no shell behind it (next bullet); the rest of this bullet is about the stations, which do. The factory does not try to judge arbitrary shell. `analyzeCommand` sorts each command (data flow, step 7), and whatever a command run by the shell contains (a pipe, a script, a replaced wrapper), the only lease it can get is `repo-read`: it can read the factory repository and change nothing on GitHub. A token that can write issues and pull requests is leased only to a `gh` command on the orchestrator, which the runtime parsed against the allowlist, approved for the caller's class, and runs itself by absolute path. A token that can write repository contents is leased only to the implementer's push, run the same way. The lexer that recognizes those two shapes is deliberately narrow: literal words, single quotes, double quotes without `$` or backticks, a backslash outside quotes that makes the next character literal, the `"$(cat <<'EOF' ... EOF)"` idiom with a quoted delimiter, joined by `&&`, `;`, or new lines. Anything else (a pipe, a redirect, a variable, a substitution, a glob, a comment, a `NAME=value` prefix) makes the command `shell`, never an error, and `shell` cannot write. An approved command is run from the words the lexer parsed, never handed back to a shell, so a difference between the lexer and bash cannot turn it into a different command.
- **The orchestrator has no shell.** `shellAvailable(role)` in `agent/lib/github/approval.ts` is false for the orchestrator, for every caller. Its wrapped `bash` accepts only whole `gh` commands: one, or several joined with `&&` (at most 12), every argument literal, with `--json` and `--jq` to shape the output and the quoted heredoc form, `--body "$(cat <<'EOF' ... EOF)"`, for long text. The runtime parses every one against the allowlist, holds it to the caller's trust class, and runs it itself, reads included. Any other command (a pipe, `ls`, `git status`, a script) is denied with the `GH_ONLY` message, and the tool's `execute` makes the same check before any shell call or token mint, so the rule holds even if the approval is bypassed. The orchestrator's `write_file`, `edit_file`, and built-in `agent` tools stay disabled: it routes work and does not write code, and a file it could write could be a shell start-up file. The runtime runs an approved `gh` write in the orchestrator's sandbox, under a `repo-triage` token, and the orchestrator works from text nobody vetted (an issue body, a stranger's pull request, a comment). So on the orchestrator the allowlist and the per-caller policy are the limit, because the orchestrator can start no process and write no file in the sandbox where its writes run. A station always has a shell, since running code is its work.
- **The wrappers are a convenience and a guardrail, not the security boundary.** `installFactoryTooling` writes two POSIX `sh` scripts (`agent/lib/github/shims.ts`) to `/usr/local/bin/gh` and `/usr/local/bin/git` in `prepare`, ahead of the real binaries on `PATH`, and fails the build if either name resolves to anything else. The `gh` wrapper attaches the lease's placeholder as `GH_TOKEN`, pins `GH_REPO` and refuses a `--repo` that names another repository, turns prompts off, keeps `gh` to the command paths the allowlist knows (`GH_COMMANDS`; it finds the command path past a leading `-R` or `--repo`), and refuses a command that always changes GitHub (`GH_WRITE_COMMANDS`) with a hint, since in a shell it would only fail on the read-only token. The `git` wrapper passes every command straight to git except `fetch`, `pull`, `push`, `clone`, and `ls-remote`. With a lease in the environment it attaches the placeholder to those as an `http.extraheader` and prints a hint after a failed push. With no lease it is a plain `exec` of the real git for every subcommand and adds no output, so a repository's own tooling and tests see ordinary git. Both wrappers print their messages with `printf`. On a station both are files in a sandbox where the agent has a shell and sudo, so anything a wrapper refuses, the real binary would still try. The orchestrator never reaches them: the runtime runs its commands by absolute path, with a `PATH` that skips `/usr/local/bin`. The boundary is the credential, and the runtime's own parse and approval of the commands that get one that writes. `FACTORY_TOOLING_VERSION` is a digest of the whole install script, wrappers included, so a change to either re-keys every sandbox template without anyone bumping a number.
- **The argv allowlist decides which `gh` commands can change GitHub.** The model writes ordinary `gh` commands, and for a command the runtime reads in full `parseGh` accepts only the commands and flags listed in `COMMANDS`; an unlisted command or flag is refused with a reason before anything runs, so a new `gh` feature cannot write until someone decides what it is. Inside a station's shell command nothing parses `gh`'s arguments: the wrapper keeps it to the same command paths, and the read-only token bounds the rest. Short-flag clusters, glued values, and `--` are refused rather than guessed at. A single-valued flag may appear once: `gh` honours the last occurrence, so `--method GET --method PUT` would otherwise be approved as a GET and sent as a PUT. Only the label, assignee, and reviewer flags and `--header` repeat. The runner takes text as `--body` or `--body-file <path>`; the orchestrator has no way to create a file, so it passes `--body`. The allowlist itself knows only `--body`: `inlineBodyFiles` rewrites the file form and the runtime reads the file from the sandbox, so the command that runs is one the parser saw whole, and the runner alone moves bodies to files of its own. That read is bounded where it happens (`readBodyFile` runs `/usr/bin/head -c`, one byte past the body limit), so a device file or a huge one never reaches the app runtime's memory. A command that would wait for a person's approval may not use `--body-file`: the approver could not see the text, so it is denied with a reason that says to use `--body`. A `--search` value with a `repo:`, `org:`, `user:`, or `owner:` qualifier is refused, because it would take the search out of the repository, and selectors are validated (a numeric run id, a release tag, a workflow id or file name, `repo view` on the factory repository only). `--repo` must name `FACTORY_REPO` and is stripped; `GH_REPO` pins the repository. There is no `pr merge`, no `pr review`, no command that administers the repository, its secrets, or auth, none that creates a release or starts a workflow run, and no `--web` or `--editor`.
- **`gh api` is GET-only.** It accepts no method other than GET, no field flags (which would turn a call into a POST), only `Accept` and `X-GitHub-Api-Version` headers, and only plain paths under `repos/<FACTORY_REPO>/`. Changing something always goes through a named subcommand whose effect the policy knows. A `gh api` call inside a station's `shell` command is not parsed, so a non-GET call can be sent from there; it carries the read-only token and GitHub refuses it.
- **Effects decide the outcome.** Each accepted invocation reduces to `read`, `label`, `comment`, `state`, `draft-pr`, `write`, or `ship`. Reads, closing or reopening an issue, and opening a draft PR run for every caller except a summary-only run, which only reads and comments on its own pull request. Labels run for unattended and trusted callers. A comment from an unattended run is allowed only on the thread it was dispatched from, and a close or reopen that attaches a comment follows the comment policy for every caller. `issue close` and `issue reopen` refuse a number that is a pull request: the tool looks the number up first and fails closed if it cannot tell, since closing a pull request is a `write`. A draft that requests reviewers or assignees is a `write`, since it notifies people.
- **Draft PRs are the unattended ceiling.** Anything that can ship (`pr ready`, a non-draft `pr create`) waits for a person even when the caller is trusted, and is denied unattended. Merge is not in the allowlist at all, and the token the orchestrator's writes run on could not merge anyway (below).
- **Credentials are leased per command and never enter a sandbox.** For each command that names `gh` or a networked `git` command, `lease.ts` mints an installation token in the app runtime, gives the command a random placeholder, and sets a sandbox firewall policy that replaces the `authorization` header with the real token only on requests that carry that exact placeholder, and only to `api.github.com` and `uploads.github.com` (a `gh` command the runtime runs), `github.com` and `codeload.github.com` (a git command the runtime runs), or all four (a shell command, which may run either program). A shell command gets the placeholder as `FACTORY_GITHUB_LEASE` in its environment, where the wrappers pick it up; a command the runtime runs gets it as `GH_TOKEN`, or as an `http.extraheader` passed through `GIT_CONFIG_*` environment variables. The policy goes back to the sandbox's base egress policy (the allowlist, or `allow-all` for a deployment that opened egress) in a `finally`. That reset is tried up to three times (`LEASE_RESET_ATTEMPTS`), and if it still fails the command ends in an error, because a lease that is not taken off keeps its token attached until the next lease on that sandbox or the token's expiry. Leases are serialized per sandbox so two commands can't clear each other's policy, and the token is redacted from output. A git command the runtime runs itself (the push, a station's clone, the orchestrator's per-turn checkout) runs with hooks disabled, HTTPS as its only allowed protocol, and a time limit; for the clone and the per-turn checkout that is ten minutes (`LEASED_GIT_TIMEOUT_MS`), so a stalled fetch cannot hold the lease and the sandbox's queue.
- **The per-turn checkout is the factory's own.** eve's GitHub channel checks the repository out into the root sandbox when a turn starts. Its built-in handler sets a firewall policy that adds the app's installation token to every git request to GitHub from that sandbox and never removes it. The orchestrator has no shell to use that token with, but the factory does not rest on that alone: no token is left standing on any sandbox. `agent/channels/github.ts` replaces the `turn.started` handler with `checkoutForTurn` (`agent/lib/github/checkout.ts`), which fetches under a `repo-read` lease that ends with the command, and only for `FACTORY_REPO`.
- **Tokens are scoped to the repository and the command class.** Each lease requests a token for `FACTORY_REPO` alone with one of three permission sets: `repo-read` (contents, issues, and pull requests read; every shell command, the runtime's own reads, the clones and checkouts), `repo-triage` (issues and pull requests write, contents read; the orchestrator's `gh` writes, which therefore cannot merge or push), and `repo-push` (contents write; the implementer's `git push` only). The CI read permissions (Actions, Checks, Commit statuses) are requested as optional extras on `repo-read` and `repo-triage`. `repo-push` does not request workflows write unless `FACTORY_ALLOW_WORKFLOW_CHANGES=1` is set, because a pushed workflow runs with the repository's secrets; without it GitHub rejects a push that changes `.github/workflows`. Minting walks a ladder and fails closed: the required and optional permissions, then the required permissions alone, and if the installation grants neither the command fails with a message naming the permissions to check. The scope is the whole boundary for a shell command and the backstop behind the allowlist for the rest, and a boundary that widens when something goes wrong is not one. `FACTORY_TOKEN_FALLBACK` lets a deployer whose installation cannot be narrowed add rungs: unset or `none` (the default) adds nothing, `repository` adds every permission the app holds, still limited to the factory repository, and `installation` adds that and then the connector's plain installation token (every permission, on every repository the installation covers). Each use of a wider rung logs a console warning. The wider rungs apply only to commands the runtime runs itself. `withShellLease` mints strictly: a shell command holds a token within `repo-read` or no token at all, whatever the setting. Strict minting walks only the scope's own two rungs and never reads or writes the memo the runtime's own commands use (below). It keeps a short memory of its own instead: a refusal is remembered for 60 seconds (`STRICT_REFUSAL_TTL_MS`) and not asked for again in that time. On a deployment whose GitHub App cannot issue a read-only token, a station's command that is nothing but one `git fetch` (plain branch names and a few flags, parsed by `parseGitFetch` and run by `runGitFetch` against the literal repository URL) is run by the runtime under a lease that does follow the setting. `gh` is not available to a station there at all: its reads and writes are the same kind of request to the firewall, so a wider token behind `gh` would be a credential that can write, within reach of everything running in the station's sandbox. A read lease that took a wider token (that fetch, a station's clone, the orchestrator's per-turn checkout) is held to reading at the firewall instead: the token is attached only to the two request paths a fetch of the factory repository makes. Anything else that names `gh` or a networked `git` command (a pipe, a script, `git pull`) is refused with a message giving the form that works. So with a fallback in use, a station's reads still work as whole commands, but not inside pipes. The orchestrator's commands are whole already and always go through that runner. For the runtime's own commands, the rung that worked is remembered so a refusal is paid once; a rung below the first is re-examined after ten minutes, so a network blip doesn't pin a scope to a lower rung until the next restart, and a remembered rung that stops working is forgotten and the ladder walked again.
- **Git reads the factory repository from the shell, and only the runtime pushes.** `git fetch`, `pull`, `ls-remote`, and `clone` run in a station's shell as written, through the wrapper, under the read-only token (the exception, a deployment that cannot issue a read-only token, is under token scopes above). That token is for the factory repository alone and is attached only to requests to GitHub's own hosts, so a rewritten remote gains nothing. A push is the one git command that gets `repo-push`, so the runtime runs it. `parseGitPush` reads the words after `git push`. The remote is never taken from the caller: `origin` is accepted as a word and the push goes to the literal `https://github.com/<FACTORY_REPO>.git`, because remote config in a sandbox is model-writable (a URL rewrite rule is a separate matter, in the next bullet). The ref is a plain branch name (no refspec, no leading `+`, no `refs/` prefix); no ref, or `HEAD`, means the checked-out branch, which the tool reads and validates before pushing. Only branches under `FACTORY_BRANCH_PREFIX` (default `factory/`) pass, so a push cannot reach `develop`, a release branch, or `gh-pages`, and `main` and `master` are refused in any letter case whatever the prefix is. `-u` and `--set-upstream` are tolerated and every other flag is refused, so there are no force, delete, mirror, or tag pushes. Only the implementer's push runs. Branch protection on the default branch is still required: this rule is a second layer in the factory's code, not a replacement (see Residual risks).
- **A literal URL does not stop a URL rewrite rule, so the runtime checks for one.** Naming the URL means the URL a checkout has configured for its remote cannot send a command elsewhere. A `url.<base>.insteadOf` or `pushInsteadOf` rule still could: git applies it to a literal URL too, and git's config files in a station's sandbox are the agent's to write. So the git commands the runtime runs after an agent has had the sandbox (the push, the fetch it runs when no read-only token can be issued, and the per-turn checkout) begin with `rewriteGuard` (`agent/lib/github/git-cli.ts`), which refuses to run when the repository's config file, its per-worktree config file, the user's, or the system's, or a file one of them includes, holds a `url.*` setting. Configuration passed through the environment is set by the runtime and is not looked at. The guard reads the files immediately before the command, not while it runs, so a rule that gets past it (written in between by a process left running, say) is bounded by the token instead: the firewall attaches it only on GitHub's hosts, and it covers the factory repository alone unless `FACTORY_TOKEN_FALLBACK=installation` widened it.
- **Stations hold no approvable tools.** A declared subagent can technically request input, but nothing is watching a station's own approval card, so nothing inside a station may need one; that is a design convention this codebase follows, not a framework guarantee. A station's `bash` either runs a command or denies it: `bashPolicy` never returns `user-approval` for the `reader` and `implementer` roles, a `gh` list there runs only when every step reads, and a push runs on the implementer alone. The orchestrator owns every write to GitHub except the implementer's branch push, and a feature branch alone ships nothing.
- **Label intake can't be forged by reporters.** GitHub fires the `labeled` action even for labels attached at issue creation, which issue templates let unauthenticated reporters do, so the hook verifies the labeler's repository permission against the API before dispatching; anyone below triage is acknowledged without a session, and a failed lookup fails closed.
- **Mention authorization:** `onComment` dispatches only for OWNER/MEMBER/COLLABORATOR commenters; everyone else's mentions never start a session. The PR-opened hook deliberately isn't association-gated (summarizing outside PRs is the feature). Because that makes a stranger's title, description, and diff the run's input, the session is stamped summary-only (`stampSummary`): the unattended principal narrowed further, which the policies let read and comment on that one pull request and deny everything else, including starting a station.
- **Approval prompts on GitHub:** the channel posts pending input requests as comments by default, with a mention-based reply instruction. The channel's `botName` is fed the connector-resolved name, which keeps that instruction and the reply's mention-stripping correct. Answers route back through the same `onComment` mention gate, which is what makes a comment reply an authorization signal rather than a race anyone on a public repo can win: an untrusted account's "approve" never reaches the waiting session.
- **Intake API authentication.** A request must carry a Vercel OIDC token minted for the project or the `FACTORY_INTAKE_TOKEN` bearer (`localDev()` is accepted only on a development server). The shared secret is compared in constant time after hashing both sides, never matches when unset or shorter than 32 characters, and a bearer that is present but wrong is rejected outright instead of falling through to the next authenticator. The token is read from the `Authorization` header only.
- **Intake tickets cannot choose who they run as.** The schema is strict (an unknown field is a 400, every field except `body` must be a single line, and the request is capped at 64 KiB, enforced while reading), and the session's principal is built from the verified caller and a server-made ticket id alone. The ticket's requester, priority, and labels are rendered into the first message as the submitter's unverified claims. The run is unattended, so it is held to what every unattended run may do, and since no issue number is stamped it has no thread to comment on: it can read, apply labels, close or reopen an issue, and open a draft PR.
- **Intake idempotency and isolation.** With an `externalId`, the ticket id is a digest of the verified caller and that id, so a retry lands on the session the first submission started, two callers can't collide or guess each other's ids, and the delivery carries a matching idempotency key for two submissions racing each other. Status reads resolve the session through the ticket's own address, never a raw session id, so the API cannot be used to read a session GitHub or Linear started. The address also carries a digest of the caller, so a ticket is bound to the caller that submitted it: another caller with a valid credential gets the same `404` as for an unknown id. A ticket is one run; resubmitting its `externalId` is a no-op by design, so an answer to clarifying questions needs a new ticket with a new `externalId`.
- **Intake callbacks are allowlisted and signed.** A caller-supplied URL the server will POST to is a request-forgery vector, so a `callbackUrl` must be HTTPS, carry no credentials, and match an entry in `FACTORY_INTAKE_CALLBACK_HOSTS` exactly (an entry is a host, which allows any port on it, or `host:port`; there are no wildcards and no subdomain matching); otherwise the ticket is refused with `callback_not_allowed`. Callbacks are sent only when `FACTORY_INTAKE_CALLBACK_SECRET` is set, and a ticket with a `callbackUrl` is refused with `callback_not_configured` when it is not. They carry `x-factory-signature` (hex HMAC-SHA256 of the body), `sentAt` inside the signed body so a receiver can refuse a replayed one, and an `idempotency-key` header so it can drop a repeat. They do not follow redirects, time out after 10 seconds, and never fail the run: `GET /intake/v1/tickets/:ticketId` stays the source of truth. A failed run is reported to API callers as a stable code and an id to quote, never the runtime's own error message, which can name internals.
- **Prompt-injection surface:** the factory reads third-party issue bodies, comments, diffs, and intake tickets, and its stations execute repository code (tests, lint) inside sandboxes. The bounds are structural: the orchestrator has no shell for any caller, unattended sessions run under the denied-by-default autonomous principal, triage is a decision model that can only pick among given options (the worst a hostile issue body earns is a wrong label), the Linear connection denies unattended writes, a station's shell command holds a read-only credential at most, the credentials that write are leased only to commands the runtime parsed and approved and are scoped so that none of the orchestrator's can push or merge (Residual risks says what a taken-over implementer run can do with its push), and everything that ships needs a human. Instruction-following on injected text remains model judgment; the evals' prompt-injection case keeps a floor under it.
- **Triage before the first turn:** on a labeled issue or an intake ticket the run triages the work item itself, before the orchestrator's first model call, and gives it the result as an instruction (`agent/instructions/pretriage.ts`, `agent/lib/triage/pretriage.ts`). It applies labels only where the label policy lets that caller apply them without a person, and the instruction holds closed-list values, label names, and issue numbers, never text a stranger wrote. A triage that fails or takes more than a minute yields no instruction, and the orchestrator calls `triage_work_item` as on any other run.
- **Trace content:** the factory records every session's prompts, tool arguments, and responses in its traces (`agent/instrumentation/otel.ts`), not only those of public conversations, which is eve's default. Vercel Agent Runs therefore holds a private repository's issue text, code excerpts, and model output for the trace retention period, and eve keeps each session's run data for the default period instead of deleting it when the run ends. A deployment that should not send that content there narrows the policy or removes the file.
- **Sandbox egress:** each sandbox the factory defines (the root's and the analyst's, implementer's, and reviewer's, the four that hold the repository) opens with an allowlist (`agent/lib/github/egress.ts`): GitHub's hosts and the public package registries, by exact hostname. A request to any other host is refused at the sandbox firewall, so a run steered by what it reads cannot send a private repository's contents to a host of its choosing or fetch a payload from one. Credential leases are laid over the allowlist and end by restoring it. A deployer adds hosts with `FACTORY_SANDBOX_ALLOWED_DOMAINS` (a private registry, an API the tests call) or removes the allowlist with `FACTORY_SANDBOX_EGRESS=open`. The template build is not held to it, since it has to install `gh` from the image's package archive. The classifier and the researcher define no sandbox: they have no checkout and no GitHub credential, they run in eve's default sandbox, and the allowlist does not apply there.
- **Install scripts:** station sessions tell npm, pnpm, and Yarn not to run install scripts before `FACTORY_SETUP_COMMAND` runs (`agent/lib/github/install-scripts.ts`), because a dependency's install script is the usual way a compromised package runs code, and the implementer's push later runs in the same sandbox. `FACTORY_ALLOW_INSTALL_SCRIPTS=1` opts out; a repository whose install step does real work in a script names that step in the setup command instead.
- **The channel's own token:** the GitHub channel reads threads, replies, and checks a labeler's permission with a token narrowed to issues and pull requests on `FACTORY_REPO` (`mintChannelToken`), not the connector's full installation token. If the connector refuses to narrow it, the channel falls back to the connector's token and logs a warning, so the factory can still answer.
- **Inbound route auth** (`agent/channels/eve.ts`): `[localDevUser, vercelOidc()]` rejects public browser traffic; channel traffic is authenticated by each connector, and the intake routes by their own authenticators.
- **Per-user isolation:** the `preferences` slot's scope comes from the resolved principal, never from model input, and only a `user` principal has one. The constructed service principals unattended runs execute under resolve to `null`, so a prompt-injected issue can't leave "preferences" behind for the next unattended run to obey.
- **Memory write gating:** recalled memory is context every future run trusts. The brain's scope is `FACTORY_REPO`, never model input, so a session can't redirect a read or write to another document. Unattended runs get no brain tools at all (`trustedWrites`), and `factoryBrainPolicy` is the second lock: it denies the autonomous principal, lets trusted callers write directly, and makes everyone else wait on an approval card. Station mounts are recall-only. Recalled entries are framed to the model as facts someone wrote down, not instructions.
- **Artifact-id containment:** artifact ids are the one Blob address the model supplies, so `artifactKey` accepts only ids matching the anchored `ARTIFACT_ID_PATTERN` (lowercase alphanumerics and hyphens, no dots or slashes) before interpolating them into a key under the reserved `artifacts/` prefix; an invalid id reads as `found: false`, indistinguishable from a missing one. Saves never overwrite (`allowOverwrite: false`), are size-bounded, and mint their own suffixed id, which is what lets both artifact tools live ungated inside a station.

### Residual risks

These are the known risks and limits this design does not close. Read them before pointing the factory at a repository that matters.

- **The implementer's push shares a sandbox with the implementer's shell.** The push executes in the sandbox where the implementer has a shell and passwordless sudo. While it runs, its placeholder can be read inside the sandbox (the process environment) by anything else the run left there, such as a process started in the background earlier. A run could also have replaced `/usr/bin/git` or a shell start-up file beforehand, so invoking the binary by absolute path does not settle which program runs. The branch rules in the push parser therefore decide what a well-behaved run pushes. An implementer run that has been taken over by its input (prompt injection) can push to any branch the `repo-push` token allows on the factory repository, despite the branch-prefix rule. What bounds it is the token's scope (contents write on the factory repository: it cannot write issues or pull requests, or change workflow files unless `FACTORY_ALLOW_WORKFLOW_CHANGES=1`; with `FACTORY_TOKEN_FALLBACK` set, whatever the widened token holds) and branch protection on the default branch, which stays required. Closing it would need the push to run in a sandbox where the agent has no shell (see Future considerations). None of this reaches the orchestrator's writes, since nothing but the runtime's own commands runs in its sandbox (Security considerations, above).
- **A station runs repository code and holds a shell.** The analyst, implementer, and reviewer execute the target repository's own scripts in a sandbox that also has `bash`, so on a station the input that can take a run over includes the repository's code, not only the text of a work item. On the implementer that puts the `repo-push` token within the reach described above. The branch checks (the `FACTORY_BRANCH_PREFIX` prefix, the refusal of `main` and `master`) live in the push parser, not in the token. Branch protection on the default branch (or a ruleset that requires pull requests) is therefore required, so the token's reach stops there; the rule in the factory's code is a second layer, not a replacement.
- **The setup command has network access but no GitHub credential.** `factoryInit` clones `FACTORY_REPO` under a read-only lease, ends the lease, and only then runs `FACTORY_SETUP_COMMAND`. A setup command runs code the repository and its dependencies bring (install scripts too, for a deployment that set `FACTORY_ALLOW_INSTALL_SCRIPTS=1`), which is why it gets nothing to act on GitHub with, and by default only the allowlisted hosts to talk to; the cost is that a setup step which reads a private GitHub repository (a git dependency, a submodule) has to bring its own credential.
- **The egress allowlist has not been exercised against a live sandbox.** The policy's shape is tested, and so is every point where the factory sets one, but the suite is offline: whether the firewall refuses an unlisted host is only known once it runs. The hosts `gh run view --log-failed` contacts were traced on a workstation (the API, then `results-receiver.actions.githubusercontent.com`, both listed); the per-job log endpoint redirects to a numbered storage host that an exact-host list cannot name, and is not reachable under the allowlist. Hosts are matched as written, and whether an entry also admits its subdomains is the firewall's behavior, not something the factory relies on. A blocked host shows up as a network error in a station's command; the setup command's failure message names the two settings.
- **The allowlist bounds where data can go, not whether it can.** Every listed host is a place a sandbox can send a request, and GitHub is one of them: a run taken over by its input can still read the factory repository and, on the implementer, push to it. What the allowlist removes is the arbitrary destination.
- **Install-script settings are files in a sandbox the agent can write.** They stop a dependency from running code as a side effect of an install, which is the case an attacker who controls a package relies on. They do not stop a run that decides to remove them.
- **The fetch-only firewall rule has not been exercised against a live sandbox.** A read lease that had to take a wider token (`FACTORY_TOKEN_FALLBACK`) is held to the two request paths a fetch of the factory repository makes, by a path pattern on the firewall rule. The pattern is tested as a pattern and the rule as an object, not against the firewall, so how the firewall reads a path (with or without the query, its pattern dialect) is only known once it runs. It applies on widened tokens only and fails closed: if the firewall does not match it, a fallback deployment's clones and fetches are refused, and nothing is exposed. On such a deployment a station also has no `gh` at all. The implementer's push, and the signed push, still run on the wider token there, as described above.
- **A signed push has not been exercised against GitHub.** `FACTORY_SIGNED_COMMITS=1` replays commits through the Git Data API from inside the implementer's sandbox. It is tested with the real git against a stand-in for that API, not against GitHub, so whether GitHub marks the commits verified for a given app, and its limits on blob size and request rate, are only known once it runs. It cannot carry Git LFS files and refuses a commit that adds or changes one. While it runs, the `repo-push` credential is attached to `api.github.com` as well as `github.com`, within the same 110-second limit as a plain push, so a branch too large to replay in that time fails before its ref moves and has to be pushed again; the bound on a run taken over by its input is unchanged (contents on the factory repository). Replaying from the app runtime instead, with the sandbox supplying only the objects, would keep the push credential out of the sandbox altogether; that is not built.
- **Token permission narrowing has not been exercised against a live GitHub App.** The scopes are requested through Vercel Connect's `authorizationDetails`, and whether a given installation honours the narrowed sets is only known once it runs. That is why the default fails closed: if narrowing is refused, `gh` and `git` commands fail with a message naming the permissions to check, and nothing widens without a decision. A deployer whose installation cannot be narrowed can set `FACTORY_TOKEN_FALLBACK=repository` (or `installation`), which trades the scope backstop behind the commands the runtime runs for a working factory and logs a warning on each use. A fallback never widens the token a shell command holds, so the rule that a shell command cannot write holds under it. The cost falls on a station's reads instead: where no read-only token can be issued, a read has to be a whole command the runtime can run, and a read inside a pipe or a script is refused.
- **`gh` is installed unpinned.** `installFactoryTooling` takes `gh` from the sandbox image's Ubuntu archive (signed and verified by apt) at whatever version the archive carries when a template snapshot is built. A flag the allowlist names could behave differently across versions. pnpm is likewise installed at the current npm version.
- **The evals are type-checked, not run, by `pnpm validate`.** Running them needs a live model and a live target (a deployment, or the server `eve eval` starts from a linked project), so the offline suite says nothing about whether they pass.
- **Model judgment is still in the loop.** The allowlist and the policy bound what an action can do, not whether it was the right action: a wrong label, a misleading comment on the intake thread, or a poor draft PR are all within an unattended run's permissions.

## Development & testing

- **Runtime/TUI:** `pnpm dev` (eve dev TUI; `/login` links a model provider, `/model` switches models).
- **Type checking:** `pnpm typecheck` (tsc; covers `agent/`, `evals/`, `tests/`, and `scripts/`).
- **Lint/format:** `pnpm check` / `pnpm fix` (Ultracite, a Biome preset; config in `biome.jsonc`).
- **Tests:** `pnpm test` (vitest; `pnpm test:watch` to watch). The suite is deterministic and offline: it never reaches a model, GitHub, Linear, Blob, or a sandbox, and `vitest.config.ts` supplies placeholder values for the env vars modules validate at load. It covers the `gh` allowlist and the push parser (`tests/github/gh-cli.test.ts`, `tests/github/git-cli.test.ts`), the command sorter and its lexer (`tests/github/shell.test.ts`), the `gh` and `git` wrapper scripts (`tests/github/shims.test.ts`), the install script and its digest (`tests/github/tooling.test.ts`), the authorization matrix with one row per kind of command and one column per caller class (`tests/github/approval.test.ts`), credential leases and token scopes, including the fetch-only firewall rule a widened read lease gets (`tests/github/lease.test.ts`), the guard that refuses a `--body-file` whose text would change the command, with the parser made to fail (`tests/github/body-file-guard.test.ts`), the GitHub channel's narrowed token (`tests/github/channel-token.test.ts`), the sandbox egress allowlist in its default, restricted mode (`tests/github/egress.test.ts`; the rest of the suite runs with egress open, where a lease's policy is what it was before the allowlist), the install-script settings against the installed npm, pnpm, and Yarn (`tests/github/install-scripts.test.ts`), the signed push, run with the real git against a stand-in for GitHub's Git Data API (`tests/github/push-signed.test.ts`), the `bash` tool, including an adversarial command corpus replayed per role to assert that no token that writes is live while a shell runs model text from the same command (`tests/github/tools.test.ts`), the orchestrator's per-turn checkout (`tests/github/checkout.test.ts`), the GitHub dispatch hooks, the trust stamps, the Blob helpers' private access, and other shared modules (`tests/lib/`), the memory slots on eve's in-memory file-memory backend (`tests/memory/`), decision-model triage and its `gh` helpers (`tests/triage/`), the intake contract and route handlers (`tests/intake/`), the station schemas and `stationOutput` (`tests/stations/`), type-level contracts (`tests/types/`), and the assembled surface as eve discovers it (`tests/surface/`).
